title: The Psychology of "Having Too Many Choices"

description.overview: Modern life offers endless options—shows, products, careers, dating, lifestyles. This topic explores how too many choices can create decision fatigue, paralysis, regret, and lower satisfaction, even when choice is supposed to feel empowering.
starters: Where do you feel the most overwhelmed by choices—streaming, food, shopping, dating, work?
Do you prefer having lots of options, or fewer curated options? Why?
Have you ever spent more time choosing than actually enjoying the thing you chose?
What helps you decide faster when you feel stuck?
Do you think social media makes choice overload worse?
examples: Picking a movie for 40 minutes and then not enjoying it
Feeling regret after buying something because you saw a better option later
Overthinking career paths or major life decisions
Using simple rules ("always pick the first decent option") to reduce stress

title: Digital Ghosts: Life After We Leave the Internet

description.overview: Our photos, posts, emails, and accounts can outlive us, creating a "digital afterlife." This topic explores what should happen to online identities, who owns them, how families access them, and whether we should curate what remains.
starters: Have you ever thought about what happens to your online accounts after you die?
Should families be able to access a deceased person’s messages and photos?
Would you want your social profiles to be deleted, archived, or memorialized?
Do you think people should leave "digital wills" (instructions for accounts)?
What feels most unsettling about the idea of a digital afterlife?
examples: A social media profile continuing to appear in "memories" or friend suggestions
Families struggling to access cloud storage or locked devices
A person scheduling messages to be sent in the future
Debates about deleting vs preserving someone’s online history

description.overview: Some people grow up between cultures—through migration, multilingual families, or deep online communities. This topic explores hybrid identity, belonging, language mixing, and how the internet accelerates cross-cultural influence.
starters: Have you ever felt like you don’t fully belong to one culture?
Do you think online communities can feel more like "home" than a physical place?
How has the internet influenced the way you talk, your humor, or your interests?
When do you find yourself code-switching (changing language or style)?
What do you think people gain—and lose—by having a hybrid identity?
examples: Using slang or memes from cultures you’ve never lived in
Feeling most understood in a niche online community
Mixing languages in everyday speech
Having different identities depending on context (family vs friends vs online)

subtopics.title: Fairness, Identity, and the Future of "Improvement"

description.overview: From memory boosters to genetic editing, human enhancement raises big questions: fairness, inequality, consent, and what counts as a meaningful achievement. This topic explores where we draw the line between self-improvement and unfair advantage.
starters: If a safe intelligence-boosting pill existed, would you take it? Why or why not?
Should parents be allowed to genetically edit traits like intelligence or height?
Do enhancements change what it means to "earn" an achievement?
If enhancements are available only to the wealthy, what happens to society?
Where would you personally draw the ethical line?
examples: Debates about students using cognitive enhancers
CRISPR-style scenarios of selecting traits for future children
Workplaces subtly expecting enhanced performance
People choosing to remain unenhanced for personal or ethical reasons

description.overview: Aesthetics—home design, outfits, desk setups, coffee rituals—have become a major way people express identity in a visual, shareable culture. This topic explores the line between genuine enjoyment and performing taste for others.
starters: Do you care about aesthetics in your space or style? Why?
What’s something aesthetic you genuinely enjoy—even if no one else sees it?
How much do you think social media shapes people’s taste?
When does aesthetic curation become "performance"?
Is having a "vibe" a form of self-expression, or social pressure?
examples: Designing a workspace to feel calm or productive
Choosing outfits for confidence vs for posting
Making everyday rituals (coffee, journaling) feel special
Feeling pressure to make your life look a certain way online

subtopics.title: How Platforms Compete for Your Focus

description.overview: In an attention economy, your focus is a commodity. Apps, ads, and notifications are designed to capture and hold attention using psychological techniques. This topic explores how that shapes habits, productivity, and well-being.
starters: What distracts you the most during the day—apps, messages, ads, something else?
Do you feel like your attention is being "harvested" online?
What tactics do you use to protect your focus?
Do you think companies have an ethical responsibility around attention design?
Is attention the most valuable currency today? Why?
examples: Turning off notifications and feeling immediate relief
Getting pulled into infinite scroll without noticing time pass
Using app limits or focus modes
Feeling more tired from information overload than from actual work

subtopics.title: Why We Laugh, and What Humor Reveals

description.overview: Humor reflects culture, values, and shared context. Memes compress meaning into layers of reference and irony, while some humor feels universal. This topic explores what different humor styles say about people and societies.
starters: What kind of humor do you enjoy most—sarcasm, absurd, dark, wholesome, slapstick?
Do you think memes are a new language? Why?
What makes humor different across cultures or generations?
Have you ever felt "out of the loop" on a joke everyone else understood?
Do you think anything is universally funny?
examples: A meme that only makes sense if you know a specific internet reference
Jokes that don’t translate well between languages
Humor as a way to cope with stress
Different generations reacting differently to the same joke

subtopics.title: Identity, Mastery, and the Thrill of the Hunt

description.overview: Collecting isn’t just about owning things—it's about completion, discovery, control, memory, and identity. This topic explores why people collect and when collecting becomes meaningful (or unhealthy).
starters: Do you collect anything (or have you in the past)? What drew you to it?
Is collecting more about the object, or the story behind it?
What feels satisfying about completing a set?
When do you think collecting becomes unhealthy?
Do you think digital collecting (like skins, NFTs, playlists) feels as real as physical collecting?
examples: Sneakers, vinyl, books, watches, trading cards, game skins
The excitement of finding a rare item
Displaying a collection as part of personal identity
Letting go of a collection during a life transition

description.overview: Cities may become increasingly "smart" with sensors, AI, and automation optimizing traffic, energy, and infrastructure. This topic explores the tension between efficiency and the messy, vibrant human qualities that make cities feel alive.
starters: What makes a city feel truly livable to you?
Do you get excited or worried about highly optimized "smart" cities?
How should cities balance efficiency with spontaneity and culture?
Would you trade privacy for safer or more efficient urban systems?
What do you think cities will look like in 20–50 years?
examples: AI-driven traffic systems and dynamic tolling
Green buildings and redesigned urban layouts
Concerns about surveillance and data collection
Neighborhoods designed for walking instead of cars

subtopics.title: Who Gets Heard When a Language Dominates

description.overview: Language dominance shapes culture, power, and whose voices are amplified. This topic explores why English dominates the internet, what might happen if another language rose, and how translation tech could change (or fail to change) global communication.
starters: Do you think English dominance online is changing, or staying the same?
If another language became dominant, what would shift culturally?
Do you trust machine translation to carry humor and nuance?
Would a world with perfect translation reduce the need to learn languages?
What’s something in your language that doesn’t translate well into English?
examples: Memes or jokes that lose meaning in translation
People feeling excluded from global conversations due to language
Translation enabling new friendships and communities
Cultural influence shifting with platform demographics

subtopics.title: Why Handmade Work Feels Meaningful Again

description.overview: In a mass-produced, digital world, many people are drawn to crafts like pottery, woodworking, analog photography, and DIY. This topic explores what craftsmanship provides: patience, tactile satisfaction, authenticity, and a link between effort and outcome.
starters: Have you ever tried a craft (pottery, cooking, woodworking, photography)? How did it feel?
Why do you think handmade work is becoming popular again?
Do you see it as nostalgia, resistance to tech, or something else?
What’s more satisfying: the final product or the process?
If you could instantly master one craft, what would it be?
examples: People taking pottery classes after years of digital work
Choosing film photography for the slower, intentional process
Buying handmade goods for uniqueness and story
DIY projects as a way to feel capable and grounded

description.overview: A conversation about the growing fatigue of performing life online, and the desire to have experiences that matter even if nobody sees them. It explores privacy, spontaneity, and whether truly "offline" moments are becoming rarer and more privileged.
starters: Do you ever feel pressure to document moments instead of just living them?
What kinds of experiences feel better when they stay private?
Have you ever intentionally avoided posting something so it stays "yours"?
Do you think privacy is becoming a luxury? Why or why not?
What would a healthier relationship with sharing look like to you?
examples: Choosing not to record a concert so you can be fully present
Keeping a trip or celebration offline on purpose
Feeling like an experience is less "real" if it wasn’t posted
Friends expecting photos/posts as proof something happened

subtopics.title: Chance, Merit, and the Stories We Tell

description.overview: A reflection on how outcomes are shaped by randomness—timing, location, connections, algorithms, and unexpected opportunities—often more than effort alone. It questions meritocracy, responsibility, and how comfortable we are admitting luck's role.
starters: Looking back, what role has luck played in your life?
Do you think society over-credits success to hard work?
Is it uncomfortable to admit luck matters? Why?
How should we talk about success without dismissing effort?
Does acknowledging luck make you feel more humble—or more frustrated?
examples: A career changing because you met one person at the right time
A post going viral and creating unexpected opportunities
Being born in a place with better schools or stability
Feeling like your work mattered, but timing mattered more

subtopics.title: Lab Food, Climate Pressure & Cultural Meaning

description.overview: A discussion about how climate change, lab-grown meat, vertical farming, and personalized nutrition could transform what we eat—and what food means. It explores a possible split between optimized health-food systems and traditional cooking as culture and community.
starters: Would you eat lab-grown meat if it tasted the same and was cheaper?
Do you think future diets will be personalized by health data?
What foods feel culturally important to you, not just tasty?
How might climate change change what your region eats?
Do you think high-tech food will replace cooking—or make cooking more special?
examples: Choosing cell-cultured meat for ethical reasons
Staple ingredients becoming expensive or rare due to climate
People eating optimized meal plans while still gathering for traditional meals
New social norms making certain foods unacceptable

title: The Slow Erosion of Local Traditions

description.overview: A conversation about how global platforms and brands can flatten local customs, styles, and celebrations—while also helping niche traditions find new audiences. It explores what gets lost, what gets preserved, and what it takes to keep traditions alive.
starters: Have you noticed any local traditions fading where you live or grew up?
Do you think the internet mostly preserves culture or flattens it?
What’s a tradition you’d want to keep alive, and why?
When does adapting a tradition keep it alive vs dilute it?
Do global trends make life richer—or more uniform?
examples: Local festivals becoming more generic or commercialized
Young people preferring global trends over traditional practices
A niche cultural practice gaining global fans online
Families intentionally teaching traditions to kids to preserve them

title: The Meaning of Home in a Mobile World

description.overview: A reflection on how frequent moves, migration, remote work, and global networks change what "home" means. It explores home as place vs people vs routines, and why some feel at home everywhere—or nowhere.
starters: When you say "home," do you mean a place, people, or a feeling?
Have you ever felt at home somewhere you didn’t expect?
Is it possible to feel at home in multiple places at once?
What makes you feel grounded when you’re in a new environment?
Do you think mobility makes people freer—or lonelier?
examples: Feeling most at home with certain friends, regardless of country
Missing a place you haven't lived in for years
Creating home through routines (coffee, music, weekly calls)
Not feeling fully at home anywhere after moving a lot

description.overview: A discussion about micro-influencers and niche creators who build small but deeply engaged audiences. It explores the benefits of intimate community and the pressures of constant engagement, authenticity, and relevance—often without major financial reward.
starters: Would you rather have 1,000 loyal followers or 1,000,000 casual ones?
Do you think micro-fame is healthier than traditional celebrity?
What pressures do you think creators feel to stay "authentic"?
Have you ever felt invested in a small creator or niche community?
Do you think micro-fame changes friendships and boundaries?
examples: A niche creator whose recommendations feel more trustworthy than ads
Feeling obligated to share personal life to maintain engagement
An audience becoming a supportive community—or a demanding one
Burnout from constant posting despite modest income

description.overview: A conversation about how technology creates gains and costs at the same time: connection and anxiety, convenience and surveillance, productivity and job loss. It treats these as ongoing tensions to navigate rather than problems with final solutions.
starters: What technology trade-off do you personally feel most often?
Do you think we can have personalized services without giving up privacy?
Has any technology made your life better but also worse in some way?
How should society decide which trade-offs are acceptable?
Do you think tech progress is mostly net-positive—or just shifting problems?
examples: Social media connecting people while increasing anxiety
Automation boosting efficiency while reducing certain jobs
Healthcare extending life while raising quality-of-life questions
Convenient apps relying on constant data collection

subtopics.title: Why Time Speeds Up or Slows Down

description.overview: A reflection on why time feels different depending on age, novelty, emotion, anxiety, and boredom. It explores the idea that new experiences create richer memories and can make life feel longer in retrospect.
starters: Do you feel like time is speeding up as you get older? Why?
What kinds of days feel long in the moment but short later (or vice versa)?
Do new experiences make life feel richer or slower for you?
How do anxiety or boredom change your sense of time?
What helps you feel more present in time?
examples: Childhood summers feeling endless compared to adult years
A stressful hour feeling like three hours
A "flow state" where time disappears during a hobby or work
Travel days feeling long because everything is new

title: How Climate Change Will Reshape Everyday Life

subtopics.title: Daily Routines Under a Changing Climate

description.overview: A practical conversation about how climate change affects ordinary life: heat, storms, commuting, outdoor time, food prices, water availability, and how cities adapt with cooling, green space, and infrastructure.
starters: Have you noticed climate effects in your daily life already?
What changes do you think will become "normal" in the next 10–20 years?
How do you think cities should adapt to heat and storms?
Do you think people will change routines (work hours, travel, housing) because of climate?
Which climate impacts worry you most: heat, floods, fires, or food costs?
examples: Planning outdoor activities around smoke or extreme heat
Rising food prices changing what people cook and buy
More indoor public spaces designed for cooling
Infrastructure upgrades for flooding and storms

title: The Balance Between Individual Action and Government Responsibility

description.overview: A conversation about where responsibility should sit for big problems like climate change: individual choices, corporate action, or government policy. It explores motivation, fairness, and how to act collectively without relying only on guilt.
starters: Do you think individual actions (recycling, less flying) matter much? Why?
What should governments do that individuals can’t?
How do you motivate collective action without shame or fear?
Where do companies fit into responsibility for climate and resources?
What’s one policy change you think would make the biggest difference?
examples: Feeling guilt about personal habits while industries pollute at scale
Debates about carbon taxes, transit, and energy policy
Communities organizing locally while pushing for national action
Policies that make sustainable choices easier by default
